participants: Chris Klevan (sales manager; addressed once on the call as "Sam")
summary: End-of-day coaching 1-1 between closer Richard Claessen and a sales manager. Richard debriefs a call he could not close because the prospect only had $50 available, and raises guilt about a second prospect (Joey, set by Derek) who did not show because Richard ran over. The manager reframes the disqualification, tells him not to feel guilty about reschedules, and gives extended coaching on presence, on closing on the call rather than letting prospects leave, and on not withholding 'the truth' from prospects. Ends with follow-up chasing on a prospect who was sent a contract and a deposit but has gone unresponsive.
notable: Manager instructs the closer to stop reading setter notes and applications before calls: 'what served me really well is not reading the notes that the setter gave and not reading the applications. Yeah, I don't read them. I ignore it.' This directly contradicts playbook check P1a, which credits 'Read back setter notes / application so they feel seen'.

Manager states a hard close-on-the-call policy and quantifies the cost of not doing so: 'You got to get them to close on the call... every time you let them off, doesn't matter how great it sounded... It's so easy for someone to just not respond to you. Probably not even. It's probably more like 1 in 100.'

Confirms deposits and contracts are used as holding mechanisms and that they frequently go dead: Richard describes a prospect sent a contract who 'hasn't even read my follow-up', and the manager asks him to chase 'that guy that sent the contract what happened to him and the deposit'.

Confirms setters brief closers and reschedule live by text: Derek texted the prospect mid-slot to ask if he could wait, then logged the no-show as a reschedule ('did you need to reschedule in that case? And then Joey responds, yes').
Manager articulates a disqualification standard on money, not intent: 'that's not an amazing set next time. So don't say that. Say, okay, great guy. No money, not a good [fit].'

Manager attributes outcomes to information-withholding rather than to fit: 'did we hold back on showing them the full scope of the truth? And if we held back on showing them the truth, then odds are, that's a big reason why they didn't have all the data they needed.'
